t: Create Grid With Exactly K Paths I
o: We must output any m×n grid of '.'/'#' where the number of monotone (right/down) free-cell paths from (0,0) to (m−1,n−1) is exactly k (k ≤ 4), or [] if impossible. Example 1 blocks nothing on a detour to yield 2 paths; Example 3 shows 1×n grids only ever have 0 or 1 paths, so k=2 is impossible. Since m, n ≤ 10 and k ≤ 4, both exhaustive search with pruning and direct construction are viable. Key facts: a 1-wide grid allows only k=1; a 2×2 grid has at most 2 paths; a 2×3 or 3×2 grid has at most 3 paths.
k: Path counts can be computed with the classic DP dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j] + dp[i][j−1] over free cells.
A 'comb' construction (free top row, free suffix of row 1, free last column) realizes exactly any k ≤ n paths.
Small boards bound the maximum achievable k, which tells us when to return [].

a.n: Approach 1: Backtracking over Grids with DP Pruning
a.i: Build the grid cell by cell (each cell '#' or '.'). After fixing a prefix, compute an optimistic path count where all undecided cells are treated as free; if even this upper bound is below k, no completion can work, so backtrack. The pruning makes the exponential search fast in practice for k ≤ 4, and it is guaranteed to find a grid if one exists.
s: Maintain a grid initialized to '#'; DFS over cell index 0..mn−1 trying '.' then '#'.
After each placement run the path DP treating undecided cells as free (upper bound).
Prune the branch if the upper bound is less than k.
At a full assignment, accept if the exact DP count equals k.
a.t: Exponential worst case (2^(mn) grids), but the DP upper-bound prune cuts the search drastically for k ≤ 4; each bound check is O(mn)
a.sp: O(mn) for the grid and DP table

a.i: Use a 'comb': free top row, free last column, and row 1 free on the suffix of columns n−k..n−1. Every path either stays on the top row and descends the last column (1 path), or drops into row 1 at some column d in [n−k, n−2] and exits via the last column (k−1 more paths) — exactly k paths whenever n ≥ k. Transposing handles n < k ≤ m. Only tiny boards need special cases: 3×3 with the center blocked gives 4 paths, and 1-wide boards or boards too small for k are impossible.
s: If m == 1 or n == 1: return the all-dot line for k = 1, else [].
If k == 1: free the top row and last column only.
Else if n ≥ k: apply the horizontal comb (top row, row-1 suffix of width k, last column).
Else if m ≥ k: apply the transposed comb; else if (m,n,k) = (3,3,4) block the center of an all-dot grid; otherwise return [].
a.t: O(mn) — we fill each cell a constant number of times

w: In an interview, present the comb construction as the main idea and use the DP only to verify your counts. Common pitfalls: forgetting 1×n / n×1 boards (only k=1 possible), miscounting the drop-at-last-column case (it coincides with the top path), and missing the 3×3 k=4 special case. Follow-ups: larger k (combine combs multiplicatively), counting grids, or proving impossibility for the [] cases.
